blocks.text: when they had set out from Persia, they had come bringing a peacock. Suidas: Μηδικὸς ὄρνις· ὁ ταώς [Mēdikos ornis; ho taōs]· The Median bird, the peacock. Likewise: Ταὼς εὐπήληξ· ὁ Μηδικὸς καὶ χρυσόπτερος, καὶ ἀλαζονικὸς ὄρνις [Taōs eupēlēx; ho Mēdikos kai chrysopteros, kai alazonikos ornis]. The well-helmeted peacock, the Median bird, furnished with golden wings, and proud. Hence Clement, Paedag. book 2, ch. 1: Ὄρνεις ἐπὶ τούτοις συνωνοῦνται τοὺς ἀπὸ Φάσιδος, ἀτταγὰς Αἰγυπτίας, Μῆδον ταῶνα [Orneis epi toutois synōnountai tous apo Phasidos, attagas Aigyptias, Mēdon taōna] [col. 137]· Besides, they buy up birds from the Phasis, Egyptian francolins, the Median peacock. And book 3, ch. 4: Ὄρνεις Ἰνδικοὺς, καὶ ταῶνας Μηδικοὺς ἐκτρέφουσι [Orneis Indikous, kai taōnas Mēdikous ektrephousi]· They rear Indian birds and Median peacocks. And Diodorus, book 2: Ἡ μὲν γὰρ Βαβυλωνία ταώνων ἐκτρέφει πλῆθος παντοίαις χρόαις ἐπηνθισμένων [Hē men gar Babylōnia taōnōn ektrephei plēthos pantoiais chroais epēnthismenōn]. For Babylonia rears a great many peacocks, variegated with colours of every kind. For although the true homeland of peacocks was India, as we prove elsewhere, they were nevertheless called Median and Persian because they were first carried from India into Persia and Media, and from there gradually dispersed into Judaea, Egypt, Greece, Latium and other regions of the world. Indeed, the very peacocks which Solomon's fleet brought into Judaea may have been obtained from Persia. For it is not likely that on that three-year voyage, by which they made their way to Taprobane (as we show in its place), they always kept a straight course. Rather, by various detours they sought out whatever served their purpose: also in the Persian Gulf, where lay the most celebrated islands of the Phoenicians, Tyrus or Tylus, and Aradus, not far distant from Persia. The name תוכיים thuccijim could also have been given to peacocks after Solomon's time, once they began to be brought overland from Persia and Babylon into Judaea.

Now, that they were called תוכיים with the letters inverted, instead of כותיים, is not without precedent, whether this happened through the carelessness of copyists or, as I believe more likely, was done by deliberate [II, 711] design, so that the name of the bird might be distinguished from the name of the people. Thus you may see the same wood called אלמוגים almugin, 1 Reg. X, 11. and אלגומים algumim, 2 Paral. II, 7. The same city in which Joshua was buried is called תמנת־סרח Thimnath-Serach, Ios. XXIV, 30. and תמנת־חרס Thimnath-Cheres, Iudic. II, 9. The same son of Dan is called חושים Chusim, Gen. XLVI, 23. and שוחם Sucham, Num. XXVI, 42. The same man is רחום Rechum, Nehem. XII, 3. and חרם Charim, in the same place, verse 15. Another is שמלי Samlai, Esd. II, 46. and שלמי Salmai, Nehem. VII, 48. So the sheep is called now כבס chebes, now כשב cheseb. And the Ethiopians sometimes invert Hebrew words entirely. Thus רחם, to have pity, is for them ምሕረ፡; קלס, to mock, for them ሰለቀ፡; זנק, to leap, for them ቀነጸ፡. Therefore, on the same pattern, peacocks could have been called תוכיים instead of כותיים. However, I propose this, I do not decide it, and I leave everyone free to judge for himself.

If the peacock were unknown, we would ask what moved Solomon to fetch from so far away, along with treasures of gold and silver, birds of no great use. Or why the sacred writers thought it worth recording? But these doubts are resolved by the appearance of this exceptional bird, which seems made for the very purpose of feasting the eyes of beholders with a delightful spectacle. Accordingly Varro asserts that nature gave it the prize for beauty among birds. And after the Greeks, who vied with one another in describing it, Tertullian paints it thus, De Pallio ch. 3: And yet the peacock too has a garment of feathers, and indeed one of the finest: deeper than any purple where the neck blooms, more gilded than any border where the back gleams, more flowing than any trailing robe where the tail lies. Many-coloured, and diverse-coloured, and changing-coloured. Never itself, always other; and yet always itself when other. In short, changed as often as it is moved. The Arabs too have toiled in the same arena, among them Alkazuinius: تري في وسط كل ريش دايرة من الذهب مخلطة بالزرقة والصفرة والخضرة وغيرها من الاوان التي [tarī fī wasaṭ kull rīsh dāyira min al-dhahab mukhallaṭa bi-l-zurqa wa-l-ṣufra wa-l-khuḍra wa-ghayrihā min al-awān allatī] [col. 138] تلايم بعضها بعضا لينشا من تركيبها [talāyam baʿḍuhā baʿḍan li-yansha min tarkībihā] You will see in the middle of all its feathers a golden circle, mixed with blue, yellow and green, and other colours which harmonize with one another, so that from their combination the highest beauty arises. He adds that gold, laid over any colours whatever, is nothing compared with this splendour, although it is scarcely dug out of the earth and only refined with much labour; whereas so beautiful a bird emerges from the egg of its own accord, without human effort. Damir has much more, which I have preferred to pass over, lest I weary the reader on a subject most hackneyed of all. So for the present it will suffice to add a few verses from an anonymous Arabic poet: [II, 712] سبحان من خلق الطاوس [subḥān man khalaqa al-ṭāwūs] * طير علي اشكاله رييس [ṭayr ʿalā ashkālihi rayīs] * كانه من نقشه عروس [ka-annahu min naqshihi ʿarūs] * في الريش منه ركبت فلوس [fī al-rīsh minhu rukkibat fulūs] * تشرق في داراته شموس [tushriqu fī dārātihi shumūs] * في راس منه شجرة مغروس [fī raʾs minhu shajara maghrūs] * كانه ببنفسج يميس [ka-annahu bi-banafsaj yamīs] *
